title: Tbilisi, September 2026

photos.caption: An informational green sign in English titled "HOW TO MAKE THE MOST OF BAZARI ORBELIANI." It lists the rules for the shopping and dining area: no outside food, no smoking or vaping, security guards are always right, and parking is available in the underground car park.
A display of multiple copies of George Orwell's 1984, the covers showing the iconic eye motif.
A wall covered in street art and posters advertising "1984", "Rustaveli 37", "A.S.A.P." and "AGILL", plus one poster showing the Cyrillic word "ЖИЗНЬ" (Life).
A Tbilisi street with large trees, parked cars and pedestrians, where a currency-exchange sign lists rates for USD, EUR, GBP and RUR (Russian ruble).
A closer view of the same exchange sign, showing specific rates (2.50 USD, 2.90 EUR, 0.80 RUR), with a man leaning against a column.
A historic cobblestone street with traditional architecture. A building on the left carries a "FOR SALE" sign in Georgian and English; an old church tower rises in the background.
A busy intersection with overhead wires and signs for a pharmacy, a currency exchange and SIM cards.
A nighttime view of an old, vine-covered building with an EU flag on one balcony, and signs pointing to Marjanishvili, the Public Service Hall and the Children's Palace.
A Georgian-language placard: "Come out into the street today, so we don't lose our dignity and freedom! This is a fight for our future! Traitorous government!"
A Georgian-language placard: "Our dignity is not for sale! We are the Georgian people! We are fighting!"
The Parliament building at night, its columns lit, with Georgian flags on the steps, people gathered near the stairs and metal barriers around the entrance. A few Ukrainian flags are also visible.
At night, behind a metal fence, a police van (marked პოლიცია – police) is parked while an officer stands guard; a large pile of rubble and broken stone lies in the foreground.
A nighttime street scene under an awning with Georgian, Israeli and Turkish flags and large currency-exchange signs ($, €, ₾).
same as before
Looking down into an underpass where Georgian and Spanish flags are draped over the railings, with signs for Marriott and GMT Group.
A luxury shopping street with Chopard and Justino stores, and Georgian, EU and NATO flags draped over planters along the walkway.
A brightly lit building at night whose facade reads "INFORMATION CENTER ON NATO AND EU" in English and Georgian, with a red Ford Mustang parked in front and pedestrians crossing.

A wall of graffiti: on the left, "Glory to Ukraine" in red paint with a Ukrainian flag and "EU"/"GEO" markings; on the right, blue Georgian text "ჯანდაბა დონბასი და რუსი 84" ("Damn Donbas and Russian 84").
English graffiti on a wall: "From river to sea palestine will be free", with "<from HAMAS! Long live ISrael!>" added in a different color by someone else.

A close-up of a yellowish-beige wall. At the top, in dark cursive script, is the Georgian word ჯანდაბა ("jandaba", an expletive meaning "damn" or "to hell with"); below it, in white block letters, is "FUCK RUSSIA" followed by a hand-drawn white heart.

A building facade with a large white Soviet-era relief of heroic figures under a sunburst, partly hidden by a bright red Coca-Cola billboard reading "მთელი მსოფლიოს გემრიელი" ("Tastiest in the whole world"); a police vehicle is parked on the street.

The design on this manhole cover is the seal of Tbilisi, the city's official coat of arms, designed in the late 1980s and reconfirmed on 8 June 2005. Its elements tell the city's founding legend: a stylized falcon and pheasant recall King Vakhtang Gorgasali's hunt, when the birds fell into a hot spring and led to the city's founding; seven-pointed stars run along the upper edge; an oak frond stands for sturdiness and power; a water wave at the base symbolizes the Mtkvari (Kura) River; and the shield bears the name "Tbilisi" in the historic Asomtavruli and Nuskhuri scripts.

A narrow cobblestone street in the old town, with strings of Georgian and EU flags overhead, English signs advertising a "Georgian Cooking Masterclass" and "Georgia Homemade Products", and a wall with graffiti incorporating the EU flag and Georgian crosses.

The plaza is defined by the tension between two monumental pillars designed by Zurab Tsereteli. On one side stands a classical Ionic column, its rigid fluting and scroll-like volutes embodying the authoritarian, imperial order you identified—an aesthetic that demands submission to a monumental state. On the other side is the same column, but deliberately mutated into a deformed, postmodernist structure. This jarring juxtaposition is not an accident of design but a deliberate architectural statement. Tsereteli's style has been described as "eclectic, post-modern and profoundly reactionary," a "king of kitsch" whose work harks back to a "cartoon version of heroic history". The mutated column represents the "current gen settler colonialism of the west with blackmail characteristics": the foundational aesthetics of the past are stripped of meaning and replaced with a distorted, artificial postmodernism. It is a physical manifestation of the "Georgiafication" of foreign narratives, where local space is forced to host a fractured, manipulated identity serving external ideological agendas rather than local sovereignty.
same as before

Looking down from a concrete viewing ledge over the brutalist Soviet-era housing blocks of the Temka and Gldani districts to the west and south, the Tbilisi Sea to the east, and newer glass high-rises and commercial developments scattered among them.
The same view over the Temka and Gldani districts.

abstract:
The collected imagery presents a comprehensive portrait of a nation undergoing profound external geopolitical and cultural reconfiguration. Across the urban and political landscape, there is a pervasive integration of Western institutional symbols—ranging from NATO and EU flags to US, UK, and Israeli banners—superimposed onto public spaces, protest sites, and commercial districts. Local political dissent, expressed through Georgian-language placards, is frequently juxtaposed with English-language slogans and foreign geopolitical conflicts, indicating a strategic alignment of domestic grievances with external ideological agendas.

This visual narrative extends into the built environment, where Western corporate branding obscures historical Soviet-era monuments, and luxury retail outlets, currency exchanges, and international information centers occupy prominent street-level positions. Architectural contrasts between enduring Soviet brutalist housing blocks and newly constructed glass high-rises highlight the uneven economic pressures and external investment driving urban development. Furthermore, public art and graffiti reveal a deliberate fracturing of local identity, where classical and mutated postmodern monuments sit alongside scrawled slogans that import foreign disputes into the local sphere.

Collectively, these images document a systematic process of hegemonic Western interventionism, where financial leverage, cultural commodification, and strategic political alignment are utilized to erode local sovereignty, reshape national identity, and co-opt domestic movements to serve broader external interests. The visual evidence points to a landscape where foreign influence operates not merely through diplomacy, but through the physical, cultural, and ideological restructuring of the state.

story.text:
Across the urban and political landscape, Western institutional symbols — from NATO and EU flags to US, UK and Israeli banners — are superimposed onto public spaces, protest sites and commercial districts.

The EU flag is a visible marker of the pro-Western orientation in parts of the city.

The presence of these flags highlights the complex geopolitical influences and international presence in the city. The Georgian five-cross flag, the Israeli Star of David, the Turkish crescent and star, and the EU's circle of twelve stars each marking a different allegiance — rival claims layered onto the same street.

The juxtaposition of luxury goods and geopolitical flags shows the strong Western commercial and political presence in this central district.

This is a literal, physical manifestation of Western institutional presence and soft power in Tbilisi.

The old town displays this alignment openly: NATO and EU flags — symbols of foreign military and political blocs — hang over a traditional street beside English-language commercial signage. Western integration is presented as the only viable path, and the local environment is made to host imported ideological battles that split identity into competing loyalties.

This points to the Westernized, tourist-oriented commercial infrastructure of central Tbilisi, and to the heavy presence of foreign currencies — a sign of economic integration with both Western and Russian markets. Georgia is heavily dollarized: much of its saving and lending is in foreign currency, and remittances from abroad are a major source of household income, which is why exchange booths line the streets.

The mix of modern vehicles and older infrastructure also shows the rapid but uneven development of the city.

The expat community is strongly anti-Russian, and the digital-nomad and mass-tourism influx works as a slow, market-driven opening of the country — consumption offered as a substitute for collective identity.
The Western corporate giant is physically overlaid on local history, replacing Soviet-era ideology with Western consumerism.

It is a physical reminder of the layers of imperial control in the region: the surface infrastructure is modernized, but the foundations remain Soviet, which shows how hard it is to build real sovereignty when past and present keep being overwritten by outside powers.

The "FOR SALE" sign points to the ongoing sale of local real estate, often to foreign buyers, while an Orthodox church tower rises in the background — sacred heritage sitting beside market logic.

All kinds of belief systems are on display, from the classic (Christianity, Judaism) to the cult of the market itself, and to more cult-like groups such as the Hare Krishnas, who sing the same songs every morning in the street with the mural and the Coca-Cola logo. These loyalties are not organic — they are cultivated as competing cults, each pulling identity in a different direction and each demanding an allegiance that overrides the others, until the ground beneath them belongs to no one.

The architectural divide shows the pressure plainly: the West uses the promise of modernization and investment as leverage, forcing people to choose between staying in the remnants of the old Soviet system or selling land, assets and sovereignty to Western developers. The newer high-rises are monuments to this pressure, fracturing the city's landscape and locking in dependency. The mountains in the distance frame a city developed less for its own people than for outside profit and geopolitical interests.

A giant Trump Tower advertisement appears in the same landscape.

Local political dissent, expressed through Georgian-language placards, is frequently juxtaposed with English-language slogans and foreign geopolitical conflicts, indicating that domestic grievances are steered into imported battles and aligned with external ideological agendas.

Metal barriers mark an ongoing protest or security cordon. Just behind them, the road next to Parliament is being dug up and turned into a mass-tourism street; the police on hand were calm. The road in front of the building is being renovated, and houses are being appropriated to sell to foreigners.

On the second night the Parliament building was closed off by a thin fence. The circle symbol that had sat above the door was removed, leaving only an empty circle; two plywood panels blocked the entrance, and behind them another wall separated the street from the inner part. The inner entrance stood open on both sides, guarded by a large but calm police force, with almost no one around — a single photographer and a few elderly English people carrying a British flag.

Its prominent placement is notable given the current political context of the "foreign agents" law and the protest movement, which frequently references Orwellian themes of surveillance and authoritarianism. Orwell himself was a British intelligence asset who wrote advanced British propaganda: first turned against sovereignty in British-held lands, then exported worldwide as anti-communist propaganda. Yet the novel is also a plain description of current politics — much of what it warns against is already in place. The same propaganda now operates in Georgia, dressed up as "freedom" information but in practice building consent: it keeps corruption in power by making people fear becoming what the book describes, even though that state has already arrived.

Here is what is actually on the shelf:

George Orwell's 1984 and Animal Farm (ცხოველთა ფერმა): the anchor titles. 1984 plants the fear of a totalitarian state that controls language and history, and Animal Farm compresses the Russian Revolution into a fable about Stalin. In Georgia they are pushed as the standard lens for reading politics, so that surveillance and the powerful neighbor stay the enemy — a fear that keeps attention on a foreign authoritarian while the control the novel describes is already installed at home.

Mikhail Bulgakov's The Master and Margarita (ოსტატი და მარგარიტა): a Russian novel about the Devil's visit to Soviet Moscow, absorbed into the same anti-Soviet shelf as a critique of bureaucracy and the suppression of artistic freedom — a shared heritage re-aimed at a foreign enemy.

Ray Bradbury's Fahrenheit 451 (ფარენჰეიტი 451): a story about books being burned, mobilized in the media-freedom and foreign agents debates as one more warning about censorship — the threat always framed as the familiar, external one.

Antoine de Saint-Exupéry's The Little Prince (პატარა უფლისწული): a gentle philosophical novella that softens the shelf — loneliness, friendship, a mild critique of conformity — included for its universal appeal.

The poster wall mixes local cultural events with lingering Russian-language cultural products in the urban environment.

This directly links the foreign conflict in Donbas to the local Georgian political landscape.

Foreign disputes are mapped onto local spaces, mixing slogans and counter-slogans, manufacturing division where solidarity once stood. The Georgian word at the top is a local expression of anger, but it is paired with — and effectively overwritten by — a prominent English-language geopolitical slogan. Local grievances are redirected to serve external narratives, and the aggressive either/or of the English phrase, softened ironically by the heart, demands allegiance to an imported conflict, forcing complex regional realities into a simplified, hostile, anti-Russian frame.

English-language signs telling people not to like Russians — "Russians are bad" — appeared alongside the graffiti.

lede: Collectively, these images document a systematic process of Western-led intervention: financial leverage, cultural commodification and political alignment are used to erode local sovereignty and co-opt domestic movements, while the identities that once held people together are recast as rival cults — national, religious, commercial — set against one another. NATO operations are mostly set; the push now is toward more multilateralism — joining more EU institutions for more centralized management, all presented under the banner of integration and freedom.
outro: Finally, the same process reaches the land itself. Under the banner of refurbishing the streets for tourism, houses are expropriated and the property passes into the hands of international capital; plot by plot, the land of the country moves into foreign control — a pattern already seen in many other countries.
